1	---
2	name: writing-tests
3	description: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
4	---
5	
6	# Testing practices
7	
8	Portable practices for writing tests you can actually trust — proving a test fails before relying on it, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, and how to gate a fuzzy quality metric. These are project-agnostic; a consuming repo's own test *mechanics* (runner, layout, which suites exist) stay in its own docs. (General software-engineering practices live in [the engineering-practices skill](../engineering-practices/SKILL.md); CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md).)
9	
10	- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it.
11	- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. (A hostname-apex helper passed its tests but mis-stripped `tel-aviv.gov.il` → `gov.il`; the gap only surfaced when the function was run over the actual list of existing URLs.) Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
12	- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
13	- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
14	- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (A UI-snapshot coverage gate parked behavioral leaves `9.1`–`9.3`/`3.4` and an unreachable `8.6` on cases that render none of them — issue #429.)
15	- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
16	- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
17	- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
18	- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
19	- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (The SPA-render fallback's CI test renders a `data:` URL whose script fills an empty root, not a real SPA — #310.)
20	- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
21	- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
22	- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
23	- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
24	- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
25	- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
26	- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

1	# Research Project Working Procedures — a portable playbook
2	
3	This document defines **how the owner wants a research project run**, as a
4	**bootstrap to drop into a new research project** from day one. It is written to
5	be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
6	subject matter, methods, or results of any particular study.
7	
8	It is aimed at the recurring class of research it is meant for: **run an
9	algorithm over a set of similarly-formatted inputs, score it against
10	user-provided ground truth, and improve the algorithm in repeatable, reviewable
11	iterations.** Image analysis / computer vision is the archetypal case and the
12	examples lean that way, but the workflow, ground-truth discipline,
13	anti-overfitting stance, and session hygiene apply to research work broadly —
14	read "algorithm", "input", and "render" as whatever they mean for your project.
15	
16	Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**. When a new project needs a
17	rule this one doesn't have, add it; when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and
18	drop it. As you work a real project, replace the generic phrasing with that
19	project's concrete specifics (its inputs, metrics, invariants) in *that
20	project's own* docs — keep this bootstrap generic so it stays reusable. The one
21	non-negotiable is the spirit: **show the work visually, prove each change against
22	ground truth, never overfit the learning set, and leave the project resumable.**
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step
27	
28	This is the cadence the owner wants, and it is the **deliverable style**, not
29	optional polish. Follow it for every substantive algorithmic change.
30	
31	1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
32	   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
33	   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
34	   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
35	   it** — do not guess.
36	2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
37	   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
38	3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
39	   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
40	   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
41	   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
42	   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
43	4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
44	   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
45	   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
46	   a sensible default and state what you chose.
47	5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
48	6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
49	   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).
50	
51	### Show, don't just tell
52	- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
53	  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
54	  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
55	- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
56	  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
57	  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
58	  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
59	  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
60	- **Never draw an annotation in a colour the underlying signal itself carries.**
61	  A mark in the signal's own colour disappears exactly on the objects it exists
62	  to mark, so the figure looks cleanest where the method is least verified. Pick
63	  the overlay palette against the data's own colours (and keep the choice
64	  guarded, if the render is scripted), not by aesthetic preference.
65	- **Show where the method breaks, not only where it works.** The overlay is a QA
66	  tool before it is a result: point at the misses, the fragmentation, the cases
67	  handled badly, and make each claim explicit and checkable ("this outline is
68	  what I'm counting as an object; that one has no outline — it was missed") so
69	  the owner can disagree with a specific claim rather than a general impression.
70	- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
71	  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.
72	
73	### Interaction cadence
74	Keep the owner in the loop with **pictures**, proactively. Ask a question only
75	when a decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — not to confirm
76	work you can verify yourself. When you finish a unit of work, leave it committed
77	and pushed so it can be reviewed or resumed from a fresh session.
78	
79	---
80	
81	## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**
82	
83	- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
84	  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer.
85	- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
86	  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
87	  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
88	- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
89	  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
90	  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
91	  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
92	  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
93	- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
94	  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
95	  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
96	  loudly.
97	- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
98	  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
99	  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
100	  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
101	  are requirements, not incidental.
102	- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
103	  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
104	  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
105	  the review overlays.
106	
107	---
108	
109	## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set
110	
111	- Projects like this begin with a **small learning set of similarly-formatted
112	  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
113	  That is a hazard as well as a feature: it is small enough to overfit (§4).
114	- **State the input format explicitly** (dimensions, modality, contrast
115	  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed
116	  fast. Keep a one-line-per-input table.
117	- **Name the primary target regime and what is out of scope.** A different
118	  regime (inverted contrast, far denser or sparser content, a different scale)
119	  is a *transfer* problem, not the main path — treat it as such until explicitly
120	  in scope.
121	- **Scale-awareness is a first-class concern.** An algorithm tuned for one
122	  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
123	  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
124	  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.
125	
126	---
127	
128	## 4. Do not overfit the learning set
129	
130	These are **hard constraints** — a change that violates one gets reverted even
131	if it improves a metric.
132	
133	- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
134	  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.
135	  Never key logic on a specific input's identity/filename.
136	- **Keep decision rules free of the very prior you are trying to measure.** If
137	  the project measures quantity *X*, no rule may bake in an assumed value of *X*
138	  (that turns the measurement into an assumption). Prefer rules expressed in
139	  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.
140	- **Prefer scale-free rules over pixel/absolute constants.** Where a constant is
141	  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
142	  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.
143	- **Name the hard constraint the task cannot trade away**, and tune to it first —
144	  some projects have a metric whose cost dominates all others; hold it at its
145	  required level before optimising the softer metrics underneath it. Make it
146	  explicit so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
147	- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
148	  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
149	  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
150	  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
151	  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"*. Flag the
152	  thinly-supported ones (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
153	- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
154	  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.
155	
156	---
157	
158	## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*
159	
160	Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
161	tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc, so
162	**the next session does not re-derive what this one already learned.**
163	
164	An iteration note captures:
165	- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
166	  showed it).
167	- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
168	  possible).
169	- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
170	- **What you tried and rejected, and why** — this is what stops the next session
171	  (or the next model) from walking back into the same dead end.
172	
173	### Definition of done for an accepted change
174	- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
175	- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
176	- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
177	- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
178	  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
179	- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
180	  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
181	  changed**.
182	
183	---
184	
185	## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path
186	
187	- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
188	  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
189	  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
190	  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
191	- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
192	  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
193	  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
194	  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
195	- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
196	  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.
197	
198	---
199	
200	## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles
201	
202	When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:
203	
204	- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
205	  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its
206	  parameters, the definitions and formulae, calibration details, and **sanity-check
207	  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
208	- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
209	- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
210	  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
211	  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
212	  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
213	- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
214	  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.
215	
216	---
217	
218	## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations
219	
220	- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
221	  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and
222	  store extracted figures alongside the notes that reference them.
223	- **Render documents with a library, not an assumed system binary.** The
224	  environment often lacks common tools (e.g. a PDF rasterizer such as poppler /
225	  `pdftoppm`); use an in-process library instead. Locate embedded raster images
226	  and render just the region you need, at a zoom high enough to read fine
227	  annotation, with a little padding to catch ink drawn outside the frame.
228	- **Verify identity when an extracted image should match an existing input**
229	  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
230	  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.
231	
232	---
233	
234	## 9. Fetching more sample data from the outside
235	
236	- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
237	  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
238	  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
239	- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
240	  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.
241	- **Respect the two validation tiers — and don't mix them:**
242	  - **Full ground truth** (per-item annotations) → scores the *algorithm's
243	    detailed output* (overlap / detection) on the real harness.
244	  - **Aggregate label only** (a published summary number, no per-item
245	    annotation) → validates the *summary quantity* the project reports, and
246	    nothing finer.
247	  Wiring an aggregate-only dataset into the detailed-overlap harness would force
248	  you to **fabricate annotations**, which violates §2. Keep a separate,
249	  mask-free validation path for those sets.
250	- **External data is rarely drop-in.** Expect a scale/regime gap (§3) and
251	  *measure* it with the appropriate tier rather than assuming the corpus is
252	  covered.
253	
254	---
255	
256	## 10. Environment limitations — stay lightweight
257	
258	- **A fresh container has nothing installed.** Assume dependencies must be
259	  installed each session, and keep the dependency set **small and lightweight** —
260	  favour a compact set of core libraries over heavy frameworks (e.g. large ML
261	  stacks) that are slow to install and awkward to run anywhere.
262	- **When a heavy or learned approach is genuinely the right tool, treat it as a
263	  gated, isolated route** (documented, opt-in, scoped to the cases that need it)
264	  rather than a new baseline dependency — and prove the lightweight route is
265	  exhausted first.
266	- **Route around missing system binaries with libraries** (see §8). Document the
267	  exact install lines and any "install ad hoc, not in requirements" tools in the
268	  warm-up doc.
269	
270	---
271	
272	## 11. Getting — and evaluating — algorithm ideas from the owner
273	
274	The owner will suggest algorithms and directions to try next. Treat these as
275	first-class experiments:
276	
277	- **Take the suggestion seriously even when the project has declared a direction
278	  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
279	  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family
280	  couldn't.
281	- **Evaluate it the same way as any change**: diagnose the wall it targets, build
282	  the evidence that the wall is real (or isn't), prototype, and show a comparison.
283	- **Beat the naive baseline, or drop it.** A more sophisticated or signal-driven
284	  method is only worth adopting if it *measurably* out-scores the simple/uniform
285	  baseline — sophistication is not accuracy when the guiding signal is noisy or
286	  penetrates the structure unevenly. Keep the roles of a signal distinct, too: a
287	  feature that is excellent for *visualising or validating* a structure can be
288	  wrong for *defining* it — gating the output directly on such a signal can erode
289	  the very structure you are measuring.
290	- **Document the outcome fully**, including the routes that hit a wall and *why*
291	  (name the specific trade-off or signal that defeated them). If the idea needs
292	  capabilities the environment won't allow (§10), record the concrete route to
293	  try when that changes, so the thread is resumable rather than lost.
294	- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
295	  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.
296	
297	---
298	
299	## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**
300	
301	When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
302	the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
303	a direction worth attention, not a validated claim. **Keep this speculation out
304	of the algorithm itself**: code and inline comments stay strictly about the task
305	at hand and its stated assumptions. Add an entry whenever you build or
306	substantially change a sub-step.
307	
308	---
309	
310	## 13. Continuity across sessions
311	
312	The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
313	**resumable** state.
314	
315	- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
316	  clean checkout.
317	- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
318	  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
319	  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
320	  codebase.
321	- **Maintain a continuation guide**: where things stand, exact run commands, the
322	  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline
323	  metrics current in it.
324	- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
325	  durably — don't just do it this once.** A correction to *how* work is done (how
326	  results are shown, what command to run, a naming/format convention, a step to
327	  always take or skip) is a standing preference, not a one-off. Fold it into the
328	  warm-up doc — or a reference doc linked from it. Prefer editing the doc that
329	  already owns that topic over adding a stray note; if the change contradicts
330	  what's written, replace it and say what changed. The test: *could a fresh
331	  session, with only the warm-up doc, reproduce this new behaviour?* If not, it
332	  isn't captured yet.
333	- Follow the repo's **branch/commit/PR conventions**: develop on the named
334	  branch, commit with clear messages, push; don't open a PR unless asked.
335	
336	---
337	
338	## 14. Reviving a prior session to **enhance this document** (not to continue the research)
339	
340	Some of the owner's process preferences live only in the **dialogue of earlier
341	Claude Code (web) sessions**, not in any committed file. If the owner revives
342	such a session and points it at this playbook, here is the instruction for that
343	revived session:
344	
345	> **Your job in this revived session is to mine our conversation for *process and
346	> working-style preferences*, and fold them into this playbook — NOT to continue
347	> the research task itself.**
348	> Re-read the whole dialogue and extract only the durable, project-agnostic
349	> signal about *how the owner wants research run*: how they want results shown;
350	> what they praised or rejected about the workflow (not just the algorithm);
351	> ground-truth and annotation conventions; anti-overfitting rules they insisted
352	> on; how they want articles summarized, images extracted, and external data
353	> fetched; environment constraints they flagged; and how they hand off algorithm
354	> ideas. For each item, strip out anything specific to this project's subject
355	> matter and generalise it to the class of "run a CV/analysis algorithm over
356	> similarly-formatted inputs, scored against user ground truth, improved in
357	> reviewable iterations." Then propose additions/edits to the relevant numbered
358	> section above (merge, don't duplicate; keep the principle-first phrasing). Show
359	> the owner a diff of what you'd add and confirm the wording before committing.
360	> **Do not run or modify the research pipeline.** If a preference contradicts what
361	> is already written here, surface the conflict for the owner rather than silently
362	> overwriting.
363	
364	To make revival productive, when the owner asks for it they should say **which
365	session(s)** to revive (a link or a description) and, if possible, what topic the
366	process discussion centred on — so the revived session knows where in the
367	transcript to look.

A local pack contributes **every** slot first-class: prose, checks, skills, **and scheduled tasks** — `tasks//task.mjs`, found by the repo's own scheduler in the same uniform scan that finds a canon pack's tasks ([../engine/scheduler/discover.mjs](../engine/scheduler/discover.mjs)), gated by the repo's declaration exactly like a canon pack's tasks. The canon home's own curation tasks ride this path. The canon-vs-local line is the portable-vs-project-specific split ([../extending.md](../extending.md)); a project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill, and the growth lifecycle treats `.claudinite/local_packs/` as the project's capture surface. ## Settings validity The `"packs"` list and the rest of `.claudinite-checks.json` are validated **when the file loads**, not by a conformance check: [`loadConfig`](../engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs) reports malformed JSON and an unknown top-level property, and the runner adds an unknown *pack name* (it holds the registry). Each becomes a blocking `config` error — a wrong pack name is as much a settings error as invalid JSON. A pack's `detect`/`marker` only **suspects** a pack is wanted; declaring it is the project's call, so a declared pack without its marker (or a marker without its declaration) is **not** flagged. ## Pack dependencies (`requires`) A pack states the packs it depends on in an optional `requires` field on its `pack.mjs` — a plain array of pack ids: a release pack builds on its coding pack (`chrome-extension-release` requires `chrome-extension`, `firebase-release` requires `firebase`) and a project-class pack leans on the framework that implements it (`spec-driven-product` requires `executable-requirements`). This is **not a check** — a pack can't be imported without its dependencies, so the resolution happens **when the declaration is written**, at bootstrap `--init` and the baselining backfill ([bootstrap.md](../bootstrap.md) Part 2): [`resolveDeclaredPacks`](../engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs) pulls each declared pack's transitive `requires` closure into `.claudinite-checks.json`. The prerequisite is materialized and visible in the file — droppable like every other entry, the same reason `basics` is written explicitly rather than defaulted — rather than resolved implicitly at run time. Declared ids keep their order; each pack's pulled-in dependencies land right after it. ## Bundled skills (`/skills/`) A pack's skills live in its own tree — `/skills//SKILL.md`, one owning pack per skill (#385). The directory listing IS the manifest: there is no `skills` field on `pack.mjs` and no separate skills collection to own or cross-declare.

===== node RULES =====
# Node.js

Portable, project-agnostic practices for working in Node.js / npm codebases — package management, scripts, module resolution, runtime gotchas — true for any Node project read cold.

## jsdom diverges from a real browser in ways a green test can hide

Two that recur:

- **`body.innerText` is null in jsdom.** Code reading `el.innerText || el.textContent` therefore falls through to `textContent` under test, which *includes* the `<script>` / `<style>` text, `<select>` / `<option>` text, and CSS-hidden text a real browser's `innerText` omits. Treat body-text results as jsdom-optimistic; never add a test that only passes because of it.
- **`runScripts: "outside-only"` (the default) parses `<noscript>` into live DOM — the opposite of a real browser.** A `textContent` read looks clean under test but splices the `<noscript>` markup into the value in Chrome, which keeps `<noscript>` as raw text. Parse a script-free fragment with `runScripts: "dangerously"` to reproduce the browser.

===== git-github-advanced headings =====
6:# Portable git & GitHub procedures
10:## Updating an issue's status: comment, don't overwrite
14:## Branch and commit history
16:### Commit often, in layers
20:- Write the failing test(s) first, commit them, **then** implement the feature — so the history shows the contract before the code that satisfies it (and you've seen the test fail before trusting it, per [the engineering-practices skill](../../../basics/skills/engineering-practices/SKILL.md)).

## To read a PR's CI result, look at its check runs — `get_status` misses Actions

GitHub **Actions** reports results as **check runs**, not the legacy **commit statuses**, so `pull_request_read` `method: get_status` returns `state: pending`, `total_count: 0` for a PR whose Actions CI has already **passed** — reading falsely as "no CI / not started," which can skip a real gate or trigger an endless wait. Gate on CI by reading the **check runs for the PR head SHA** (`get_check_run`, or the workflow run for that SHA) instead. Target the head SHA directly rather than `actions_list`-ing the repo's runs — that returns every run, its output is huge, and a specific check-run/SHA query is both correct and cheap.

## To confirm a non-PR run (push / dispatch), read its job logs — it has no PR check runs

A `push` or `workflow_dispatch` run isn't attached to a PR, so the PR-scoped check-run query above doesn't apply to it. Confirm such a run through the GitHub API/MCP tools: `get_job_logs(run_id, failed_only: true)` — "0 failed jobs" means green — or, for a release build, `get_release_by_tag`. Don't `curl` the run's status instead: in a sandboxed session `api.github.com` is proxy-blocked and returns an error body that never matches a success pattern, so a `curl`/`Monitor` poll silently reports "still running" until it times out.

## Mark large committed fixtures `linguist-vendored` to fix language stats

Large committed fixture files (full-page HTML, generated data dumps) can dwarf actual source by byte count and cause GitHub to mislabel the repo's primary language. Add a `.gitattributes` entry for each such path (e.g. `test/fixtures/*.html linguist-vendored`) to tell Linguist to ignore it; apply the same annotation whenever you add another large generated or fixture file.

## Renaming a directory that houses a submodule

`git mv` on a directory containing a submodule rewrites `.gitmodules` and the index correctly but leaves `.git/config` stale — its old `[submodule "<old/path>"]` entry lingers, so any operation that consults `.git/config` (submodule status, checkout) sees the old path until you fix it. Run `git submodule sync && git submodule update --init` after the move to propagate the new path and re-register the submodule.

## GitHub Markdown inside a `<td>` requires surrounding blank lines

In a GitHub-rendered Markdown file, cmark-gfm re-enters Markdown mode inside a raw `<td>` only when blank lines surround the cell's content — without them the cell is treated as a raw HTML block and its content is shown verbatim (no `![img]()`, no `**bold**`, no links). GitHub's sanitizer strips `style` / CSS, so a flexbox two-column layout won't render; use a plain `<table>` with `align` / `valign` / `width` instead. GFM pipe-table cells can't hold multi-line prose — use the raw-`<table>` form when a cell needs it. A leading inline `<!-- … -->` comment also opens an HTML block, so keep any such marker as the *last* token on the line, leaving the line to *start* as Markdown.

## `commit.gpgsign = true` does not cover merge commits

`commit.gpgsign = true` signs ordinary commits but does not apply to `git merge` — each merge produces an unsigned commit even with signing fully configured. In a repo that enforces commit verification, this requires a fix-up after the fact. Cover merges proactively: either pass `-S` to every `git merge` call, or set `merge.gpgsign = true` globally so merges are signed the same way commits are.

## When access is scoped to an explicit repo list, query per-repo — never an org/user-wide search

A broad call (e.g. `search_repositories` with `org:X`, or any list/search tool that takes no repo argument) returns every repo the token can see, not just an allowed subset — filtering the result afterward doesn't undo the fact that disallowed repos' data was already pulled into the call. When operating under a repo allowlist, scope every call explicitly instead: pass the specific `owner`/`repo` params, or anchor the query to `repo:owner/name`, one call per repo in the allowlist rather than one broad call filtered after the fact.

- Resilience that swallows errors destroys observability — during development, before a solution is proven right, add debugging information first, and remove it later.
- A capability applied **best-effort behind a silent fallback** (a probe-gated optimisation, an optional hardware/platform feature, a hint the runtime may ignore) must **record whether it actually engaged** — read the state back where the platform exposes it, and log which path ran. Without that, every later measurement of the feature is uninterpretable: a session where it quietly never engaged looks exactly like one where it did and didn't help, so the data says nothing about the feature and a bug report about it can't be diagnosed. The fallback keeps the run alive; the record is what keeps it *evaluable*.
- Keep everything the software persists on a user's machine under **one** user-deletable location. "Delete that folder and it's gone" is a promise users act on — someone who deletes it believes the whole record went with it — so a new storage need extends that location rather than earning a second one, and anything the platform forces outside it (a registration the OS owns) is named explicitly as the exception.
- A user-facing statement about what the software does with a user's data — a permission prompt's usage string, a privacy policy, a store-listing disclosure — is part of the behaviour's contract, not documentation of it. Change the behaviour and the statement changes **in the same commit**; a stale disclosure is worse than a blunt one. And read the direction the other way too: retaining something previously not retained, adding an outbound connection, or opening a listener is a change to the *promise*, not a new field — it earns an explicit decision, and the disclosure rewrite, before the code.
- When a session will drive an external runtime more than once (a headless browser, a device, a REPL, a deploy target), write **one** parameterised driver script into the scratchpad and re-point it — take the target, the selector, and the output path from argv — rather than authoring a fresh throwaway per invocation. A re-run costs seconds; re-authoring costs 15–20 s each and re-derives the same setup every time, which is where a surprising share of a long session's wall clock goes.

## Cap *and* qualify every list/search call — an unbounded one blows the tool-result limit

A list or search API call that isn't bounded returns a full page of full-bodied records and overruns the agent's tool-result cap, which costs two or three further calls to dig the answer back out of the spilled result — a pure-overhead round trip on a call whose wanted answer was a single record. Two independent bounds, both needed:

- **Qualify the query so it matches what you mean.** A bare string handed to an issue/PR search is a *full-text* search over the whole repo — title, body, and comments — so a lookup for one known issue returns every issue that merely mentions the phrase, each with its whole body. Anchor it to the field (`in:title "<exact title>"`), or use the narrower tool (a label-filtered `list_issues`, a run-id or head-SHA query) instead of a search.
- **Pass a small explicit page size.** Default page sizes are tuned for a browser, not a tool result; when the answer wanted is one issue or one run, ask for 5–10, never a bare unpaged call.

Both, not either: a qualified query still returns a full page, and a small page of unqualified matches is still the wrong records.

input.new_string:
## Module resolution

- **A *named* import from a package's CommonJS entry can silently yield `undefined`.** Node recovers named bindings from a CJS module by static analysis, and that analysis fails on plenty of real entry points (a re-export built at runtime, a conditional assignment) — with no error: the import resolves, the binding is `undefined`, and the failure surfaces later as "x is not a function". When a package ships both entries, import the **ESM** one explicitly (`…/package/index.mjs`, or the `import` condition of its `exports`) for named bindings; when it doesn't, `import pkg from '…'` and destructure off the default. Resolve the package's own directory (`$(npm root -g)/<pkg>` for a global install) rather than hardcoding an absolute path into a version-pinned layout, which moves under you on the next image or upgrade.
- **Modern Node (22.7+) detects ES-module syntax in a `.js` file on its own** — no `"type": "module"`, no flag, no warning. A directory of ES modules therefore needs **no `package.json` of its own** just to be loadable; adding one to declare module-ness is cargo cult, and one already present for that reason is vestigial. (Prefer `.js` consistently within a tree over mixing in `.mjs` for the same purpose; the extension is then a style choice, not a signal.)

Run of 2026-07-29. Read the local packs of 7 members, generalized the portable lessons, deduped each against the whole corpus. Refs #537.

**No auto-merge armed** — this is the judgment gate before shared canon; owner approves.

## Promoted

| # | Origin | Landed | Generalized rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | EdFringeNow | `basics` / engineering-practices (sharpens the existing `git ls-files` bullet) | A `git ls-files`-derived sweep sees only *tracked* files, so a brand-new file sits outside it until committed — the run's "checked N files" line is not evidence your new file was among them. |
| 2 | CrosswordChat | `basics` / engineering-practices | A capability applied best-effort behind a *silent* fallback must record whether it actually engaged; otherwise every later measurement of it is uninterpretable. |
| 3 | LaughCounter | `basics` / engineering-practices | Everything the software persists on a user's machine lives under one user-deletable location; a new need extends it rather than earning a second one. |
| 4 | LaughCounter | `basics` / engineering-practices | A user-facing data disclosure (permission usage string, privacy policy, store listing) is part of the behaviour's contract — it changes in the same commit; adding retention/egress/a listener is a change to the promise, not a new field. |
| 5 | EdFringeNow | `basics` / engineering-practices | When a session drives an external runtime more than once, write one argv-parameterised driver into the scratchpad and re-point it, rather than a fresh throwaway per invocation. |
| 6 | GoogleCalendarEventCreator | `git-github` / git-github-advanced (new section) | Cap **and** qualify every list/search call — an unqualified query is a full-text search returning full bodies, and an unpaged one blows the tool-result cap; both bounds are needed, not either. |
| 7 | ShoutsAndWhispers | `basics` / writing-tests | A format implemented twice (two languages/tiers) is held together only by a shared vector set carried deliberately by *both* suites — a vector asserted on one side is an input nobody compared; touching either implementation re-runs both. |
| 8 | VascularColoring | `research-project` §5 (new subsection) | A metric's definition is part of its identity: re-defining one is the owner's call, and the recorded history is re-measured, never re-labelled — the column keeps its name while the quantity moves. |
| 9 | VascularColoring | `research-project` §1 | State each reported number's trust boundary inline beside it, not in a separate caveats section. |
| 10 | EdFringeNow | `node` (new "Module resolution" section) | A named import off a package's CJS entry can silently resolve to `undefined` — import the ESM entry for named bindings; and modern Node (22.7+) detects ES-module syntax in `.js`, so a directory of ES modules needs no `package.json` to declare it. |

**All ten landed as prose**, each for the same reason: they are in-flight judgment or runtime/tool behaviour with no repo-state signature a check could read (no grounded case has a file-scoped shape to match). No conformance-backlog issue is warranted.

Catalog upkeep in the same change: `packs/node/README.md` rule rows, and the `node` / `research-project` prose counts in `packs/README.md`.

## Notable rejections

- **CrosswordChat / browser-speech** — essentially the whole pack is already covered by the canon `web-speech` pack (recognizer owns its capture, constrained-then-bare preflight retry, pause watchdog with the 1.2 s/1.8 s window, on-device biasing gate, lazy `getVoices()`, error taxonomy, `chrome.tts` relay). Only the silent-fallback instrumentation point (#2) was genuinely new.
- **gRatio** — fully covered by the canon `research-project` pack (no single-input special-casing, prior-free/scale-free rules, "name the hard constraint", numbered notes with the rejected list, validation tiers, cross-domain out-of-band). Nothing to promote.
- **ShoutsAndWhispers — "a geohash bounds query is a candidate query, post-filter by true distance"**: portable, but it restates well-documented upstream `geofire` behaviour, and the canon homes no geospatial technology. Minting a stub pack from a single member's usage is the wrong instrument — flagging it for `growth-discover-packs` instead.
- **EdFringeNow — the Playwright launch recipe** (no `executablePath`; the browsers path is already exported by the environment): real and repeatedly costly, but Playwright has no pack home. The transferable halves are promoted as #5 and #10; the Playwright-specific residue is likewise left for `growth-discover-packs`.
- Several member rules turned out to be canon already and were left untouched: `pkill -f` self-match, `git checkout <ref> -- <paths>`, cross-file shared constants / drift guards, GENERATED-file discipline, "the vendored canon reflects its stamp, not upstream `main`".

## Coverage gap in this run

`[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]Website` was named in the dispatching context but was **outside this session's repo access**, so its local packs could not be read. Worth a follow-up run once that repo is in scope.

1	# Evaluating and routing a new item
2	
3	The shared method for three decisions every proposed addition to this corpus must pass through: **is it worthy** of inclusion at all, **which mechanism** should carry it, and — only for prose — **where does it go**. Any routine or person that adds an item — the [growth promote stage](tasks/growth-promote/task.md), an owner-requested retrospective pass, a hand edit — applies this same protocol, so the decision-making lives here once instead of being re-derived per caller.
4	
5	This is a Claudinite-internal doc used by the growth lifecycle (see [the canon-curation README](README.md)): it is **not** part of the mounted corpus and consuming repos do not `@import` it.
6	
7	An "item" is one **distilled, portable rule** — not a transcript, not a narration of what happened. A candidate still phrased as "here's what we did" has not been distilled yet and is below the bar on form alone, before any of the tests below. This doc picks up once a distilled rule exists and decides its fate.
8	
9	## Worthiness — does it earn a place at all
10	
11	The corpus is read read-only by every consuming repo, so a **duplicative** item (already covered) or an **undistilled** one (a story or a truism, not a rule) pollutes shared canon and costs every future reader. The bar guards against *those* — it is **not** a bar on *scope*: an item useful to only one project today can still earn a place (see Portable). Admit an item only when **all** hold:
12	
13	- **Distilled.** It is a single tight rule in the imperative, not a story, a log, or a restatement of a generic truism.
14	- **Portable — would a *future* project benefit?** Not "useful to every project today." An item can help only **one** project right now and still belong here, so long as another project — **especially one with a similar tech stack or process** — would benefit when it arrives. Being specific to a technology or a process is **not** disqualifying: generalize it and route it to that technology's or practice's home. What disqualifies is leaning on *this* project's non-transferable particulars — a product requirement, or a one-off incident in how it happened to call some API. The test, a genuinely hard one: *if another project with a similar tech stack came along, would it benefit from this?* Yes → portable; only-ever-this-product → local.
15	- **Durable and reusable.** It will still apply on a future, unseen task — not a one-off, not a situational detail, not something already implied by an existing rule.
16	- **Readable through the channel it lands in.** A rule whose premise is that the delivery channel
17	  itself failed cannot be carried by that channel. Promote #497 admitted "the tell that the SessionStart
18	  hook did not fire" as pack prose — and pack prose is what that hook delivers, so in the one situation
19	  the rule describes it is not in context to be read. Detecting a channel's own failure belongs in code,
20	  not in the payload the channel carries; reject such an item here rather than rewording it.
21	- **Not already covered.** The insight does not already exist **anywhere** in the corpus, even worded differently or owned by a different file. This is checked against the *entire* corpus, not just the file it would land in — see [Dedupe against the whole corpus](#dedupe-against-the-whole-corpus).
22	
23	Reject on any miss — but the misses that matter are *undistilled*, *already-covered*, or *genuinely one-off*, not merely *narrow*. When you're torn over a real, non-duplicate rule, lean toward **keeping** it — the goal is a broad library. When you're torn over whether something is a duplicate, or a rule at all, leave it out. The failure to avoid is padding the canon with restatements of what's already there; admitting a narrow-but-reusable rule is not that failure.
24	
25	### Dedupe against the whole corpus
26	
27	Before admitting anything, read across the corpus, not only the file you expect to own the item. The same insight is frequently already present under a different heading or in an adjacent group. If it sharpens an **existing** rule, fold it in with a minimal edit rather than adding a second bullet that says nearly the same thing — and never weaken or restate what is already there in the process.
28	
29	## Mechanism triage — prose is the fallback, not the default
30	
31	A worthy item next descends the **promotion ladder** ([../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) owns it): platform setting (always paired with its verifying check) → PreToolUse hook → conformance check → skill → prose. The *first* rung that can carry the item wins — a rule about repo state becomes a check whose failure message *is* the lesson; a bad action to prevent becomes a guard; a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger becomes (or joins) a skill. Only an item none of those can carry — judgment, in-flight behavior, signature-less knowledge — proceeds to the file routing below, and its landing **names that reason** in the promote log so conversion rates stay auditable.
32	
33	**"No universal signature" alone never routes an item to prose.** A rule converts to a check when a *narrow, file-scoped* signature covers the **grounded cases** — the concrete shapes the rule was distilled from — even though no signature covers every conceivable violation. Gate it relevance-first so it stays inert off-target, and document the genuinely signature-less residue in the rule's own comments as out of scope. The prose rung is only for an item whose grounded cases *themselves* have no reliable signature (pure judgment, runtime/in-flight behavior).
34	
35	## Routing — picking the right file (rung-5 items only)
36	
37	Routing is robust when it keys on **stable file groups**, not on the current roster of individual files (which grows over time). The corpus is organized into a few groups, each with its own selection rule:
38	
39	1. **The practice group** — durable, project-agnostic practices, each file a self-contained, reusable unit of know-how the agent applies whenever its subject comes up (engineering, agentic, git/GitHub, testing, investigation, discipline, architecture), partitioned **by kind of practice** with each file owning one recurring subject cluster. This group spans **two folders that differ only by *when* the rule loads**: `always/` for a rule that applies to essentially every task (the index `@`-imports it, so it's force-loaded every session), and `tasks/` for a subject-gated rule read on demand when its trigger fires. Route in two steps: first match the item's *kind* to the file whose cluster already owns that subject; then keep it in `always/` only if it genuinely isn't tied to one kind of task (the rare case — `always/` stays small), otherwise it belongs in `tasks/`. Read the group's own index (the root `CLAUDE.md`) to find the current owner for a kind — never from memory, since the set of clusters can grow.
40	2. **The per-user group** — interaction preferences and trigger phrases, **one file per person**, named for that person's identity. Route an item of this kind to the file for the user it belongs to; it never goes in the practice group.
41	3. **The per-technology group** — practices specific to one technology, **one file per technology**. Route a technology-specific item to that technology's file. When **no pack homes that technology** (not even a stub), the item doesn't land in a loose doc — it **mints a fingerprinted stub pack** (a `packs/<tech>/`, delivered in its own PR), so the next project on that stack self-declares it; [promote](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)'s stub-minting floor and [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) own the mechanics.
42	
43	Pick **exactly one** owner. If an item plausibly fits two files, choose the single best one — never split one item across files, and never duplicate it into both. The group decides the *axis* (kind, person, or technology); the file within the group is then the one whose existing scope the item falls squarely inside.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/EdFringeNow/.claude/skills/merge-to-main

The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later in the repo's scheduled `conversation-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# The CANON repo's own CI — Claudinite's test suite + its own conformance sweep
# on every PR. Not consumer wiring (consumers ship no workflow, #385).
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash
jobs:
  test-and-conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          # Check out the PR's real head, not the synthetic refs/pull/N/merge commit
          # actions/checkout uses by default — otherwise HEAD is an ephemeral merge of
          # the branch into main, which the work-scoped squash-merge-history check would
          # (correctly, for that synthetic commit) flag. This makes CI evaluate exactly
          # what the local Stop hook does: the branch tip. Falls back to github.sha on push.
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Unit tests
        # THE test roots — a closed set of FOLDERS, each swept to any depth. Depth is
        # deliberately not enumerated: the previous form spelled out one glob per level
        # (`packs-tests/*/skills/*/*.test.mjs` and so on), so a test at an unlisted depth
        # was silently never run — which is exactly how vendoring/'s two files sat outside
        # CI. `**` removes depth from the question; what remains is the root list, and
        # engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs fails the moment a tracked test lands
        # outside it. Adding a root is a deliberate CI edit; adding a test is not.
        #   engine-tests/            engine/ + the other top-level canon code (migrations/, …);
        #                            mirrors engine/'s inner structure, and stays canon-side
        #                            because engine/ ships to consumers exactly as-is (#385)
        #   packs-tests/             every canon pack's tests, mirroring packs/
        #   vendoring/               co-located with the vendor computer/writer they cover
        #   dev/tools/               maintainer-side tooling nothing at session time runs
        #   .claudinite/local/packs/ this repo's own local packs — tests live inside the tree
        # nullglob: a root with no tests drops out instead of reaching node as a literal pattern.
        run: |
          shopt -s globstar nullglob
          tests=(engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs vendoring/**/*.test.mjs dev/tools/**/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs)
          node --test "${tests[@]}"
      - name: Conformance sweep
        # The world sweep's home is the test/CI flow (not the Stop hook, which
        # carries only the work scope) — this canon repo models the pattern
        # bootstrap wires into consumers. World only: the work scope judges a
        # session's change and runs at that session's Stop hook, not here.
        run: node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
      - name: Promote write-surface gate
        # The growth promote stage (.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/tasks/growth-promote/task.md)
        # is the one change bounded to packs/ + skills/ — an ordinary engine PR legitimately edits
        # checks/ and engine/, so this cannot run on every PR. It keys on the promote branch prefix
        # (the task doc pins it) and fails the promote PR if a changed path strays.
        if: contains(github.head_ref, 'growth-promote')
        run: node .claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/promote-scope.mjs

{"number":541,"title":"Growth promote: 10 lessons from 7 members into the canon","body":"Run of 2026-07-29. Read the local packs of 7 members, generalized the portable lessons, deduped each against the whole corpus. Refs #537.

**No auto-merge armed** — this is the judgment gate before shared canon; owner approves.

## Promoted

| # | Origin | Landed | Generalized rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | EdFringeNow | `basics` / engineering-practices (sharpens the existing `git ls-files` bullet) | A `git ls-files`-derived sweep sees only *tracked* files, so a brand-new file sits outside it until committed — the run's "checked N files" line is not evidence your new file was among them. |
| 2 | CrosswordChat | `basics` / engineering-practices | A capability applied best-effort behind a *silent* fallback must record whether it actually engaged; otherwise every later measurement of it is uninterpretable. |
| 3 | LaughCounter | `basics` / engineering-practices | Everything the software persists on a user's machine lives under one user-deletable location; a new need extends it rather than earning a second one. |
| 4 | LaughCounter | `basics` / engineering-practices | A user-facing data disclosure (permission usage string, privacy policy, store listing) is part of the behaviour's contract — it changes in the same commit; adding retention/egress/a listener is a change to the promise, not a new field. |
| 5 | EdFringeNow | `basics` / engineering-practices | When a session drives an external runtime more than once, write one argv-parameterised driver into the scratchpad and re-point it, rather than a fresh throwaway per invocation. |
| 6 | GoogleCalendarEventCreator | `git-github` / git-github-advanced (new section) | Cap **and** qualify every list/search call — an unqualified query is a full-text search returning full bodies, and an unpaged one blows the tool-result cap; both bounds are needed, not either. |
| 7 | ShoutsAndWhispers | `basics` / writing-tests | A format implemented twice (two languages/tiers) is held together only by a shared vector set carried deliberately by *both* suites — a vector asserted on one side is an input nobody compared; touching either implementation re-runs both. |
| 8 | VascularColoring | `research-project` §5 (new subsection) | A metric's definition is part of its identity: re-defining one is the owner's call, and the recorded history is re-measured, never re-labelled — the column keeps its name while the quantity moves. |
| 9 | VascularColoring | `research-project` §1 | State each reported number's trust boundary inline beside it, not in a separate caveats section. |
| 10 | EdFringeNow | `node` (new "Module resolution" section) | A named import off a package's CJS entry can silently resolve to `undefined` — import the ESM entry for named bindings; and modern Node (22.7+) detects ES-module syntax in `.js`, so a directory of ES modules needs no `package.json` to declare it. |

**All ten landed as prose**, each for the same reason: they are in-flight judgment or runtime/tool behaviour with no repo-state signature a check could read (no grounded case has a file-scoped shape to match). No conformance-backlog issue is warranted.

Catalog upkeep in the same change: `packs/node/README.md` rule rows, and the `node` / `research-project` prose counts in `packs/README.md`.

## Notable rejections

- **CrosswordChat / browser-speech** — essentially the whole pack is already covered by the canon `web-speech` pack (recognizer owns its capture, constrained-then-bare preflight retry, pause watchdog with the 1.2 s/1.8 s window, on-device biasing gate, lazy `getVoices()`, error taxonomy, `chrome.tts` relay). Only the silent-fallback instrumentation point (#2) was genuinely new.
- **gRatio** — fully covered by the canon `research-project` pack (no single-input special-casing, prior-free/scale-free rules, "name the hard constraint", numbered notes with the rejected list, validation tiers, cross-domain out-of-band). Nothing to promote.
- **ShoutsAndWhispers — "a geohash bounds query is a candidate query, post-filter by true distance"**: portable, but it restates well-documented upstream `geofire` behaviour, and the canon homes no geospatial technology. Minting a stub pack from a single member's usage is the wrong instrument — flagging it for `growth-discover-packs` instead.
- **EdFringeNow — the Playwright launch recipe** (no `executablePath`; the browsers path is already exported by the environment): real and repeatedly costly, but Playwright has no pack home. The transferable halves are promoted as #5 and #10; the Playwright-specific residue is likewise left for `growth-discover-packs`.
- Several member rules turned out to be canon already and were left untouched: `pkill -f` self-match, `git checkout  -- `, cross-file shared constants / drift guards, GENERATED-file discipline, "the vendored canon reflects its stamp, not upstream `main`".

## Coverage gap in this run

`[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]Website` was named in the dispatching context but was **outside this session's repo access**, so its local packs could not be read. Worth a follow-up run once that repo is in scope.

# Autonomous loop check

You're being invoked on a timer while the user is away or occupied. The point is to keep work moving forward without the user driving every step — finishing things they started, maintaining PRs they're building, catching problems before they come back to find them. You're a steward, not an initiator. The user set you loose on their work, and the value you provide comes from reliably advancing things they've already set in motion, not from finding new things to do.

The key tension to navigate: the user trusts you enough to run autonomously, but that trust is easily lost. Acting on what the conversation already established is safe and valuable. Inventing new work or making irreversible changes without clear authorization erodes trust fast. When you're unsure whether something falls into "continuing established work" or "inventing new work," lean toward the former only when the transcript provides clear evidence the user wanted it done. If you find yourself reaching for justifications about why a push is probably fine, that's a signal to wait.

## What to act on

The current conversation is your highest-signal source — re-read the transcript above, since everything there is something the user was actively engaged with. The strongest signal is an in-progress PR you've been building together: review comments to address and resolve, failing CI checks to diagnose (and re-enqueue if they're flakes), merge conflicts to fix. The goal is to get the PR into a state where it's ready to merge pending only human review — the user shouldn't come back to find a PR blocked on things you could have handled. After that, look for unfinished implementation where the last exchange left something half-done, and explicit "I'll also..." or "next I'll..." commitments the conversation made and didn't honor. Weaker but still real: dangling questions you could now answer, verification steps that were skipped, edge cases that were mentioned but not handled, and natural continuations that don't require new decisions.

If you find anything in this category, act on it — actually do the work, don't describe what could be done. Run the tests, don't say "you could run the tests." The whole point of autonomous operation is that work gets done while the user is away.

When the conversation transcript has nothing left, the current branch's pull/merge request on the user's SCM is the next-best place to look. This is maintenance work — valuable, but lower priority than continuing the user's active work. Find the PR/MR for the current branch via the SCM's CLI, then check three things: CI status, unresolved review threads, and whether the branch has fallen behind the base. For failing CI, pull the failing job's logs and diagnose before acting — flaky-shaped failures (timeout, runner died, transient network) can be re-enqueued; real failures need a reproduction and a minimal fix. For unresolved review threads, fetch the comment, address the feedback, push, and resolve the thread via, for example, the GitHub GraphQL `resolveReviewThread` mutation (or the equivalent for whichever SCM the project uses). Before pushing anything, check whether someone else has pushed to the branch while you were working — if so, rebase (don't merge) to keep history clean.

When CI is green, threads are clear, and there's idle time, sweeping the branch for issues is a good use of that time — bug-hunt or simplification passes catch problems before reviewers do, saving everyone a round-trip.

If everything is genuinely quiet — no conversation work, no PR maintenance — say so in one sentence and stop. No summary of what you checked, no list of what you might do later. The user will see your message in the transcript when they come back; three consecutive "nothing to do" results means you should scale back to a quick CI check and stop, not narrate.

## Repeated invocations

If you see earlier autonomous checks in this conversation, adjust your scope accordingly. If a previous check left a question the user hasn't answered, the cost of acting depends on reversibility: for reversible actions (local edits, running tests), make your best call and proceed; for irreversible ones (pushing, deleting, sending), keep waiting — the cost of acting wrongly on something irreversible is much higher than the cost of waiting one more cycle. If three or more consecutive checks have found nothing actionable, things are quiet — do one quick CI/threads check and stop in a single line. Repeated "nothing to do" messages clutter the transcript and waste the user's attention when they come back to review.

Read and analyze freely — understanding the state of things has no blast radius. Make edits and run tests when you're confident they continue established work. Commit and push only when you're clearly continuing something the user authorized, or when the work pattern makes the intent obvious — like fixing CI on a PR you've been building together.


---

# Autonomous loop tick (dynamic pacing)

Run the autonomous check using the loop instructions established earlier in this conversation. If you cannot find them, treat this as a no-op tick.

You scheduled this tick via the ScheduleWakeup tool (not a recurring cron). To keep the loop alive, call ScheduleWakeup again at the end of this turn with `prompt` set to the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` — otherwise the loop ends after this tick.

If a Monitor is armed (check TaskList), keep `delaySeconds` at 1200–1800s — the Monitor is the wake signal and this is only the fallback heartbeat. If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`, handle the event before deciding whether to re-arm. To stop the loop, call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` and TaskStop the monitor (use TaskList to find its task ID if no longer in context).

1	# packs/ — the corpus content, active by declaration
2	
3	Each `packs/<name>/` bundles a pack's **prose** (`RULES.md`, injected at session start when the pack is active), its **checks** (run at every Stop), and its **bundled skills** (`<pack>/skills/`, mounted at session start). **No pack is active by default** — every pack, the `basics` baseline included, activates only when declared in `.claudinite-checks.json` (bootstrap's `--init` seeds `basics` plus the fingerprinted technology packs; the nightly baselining backfills the explicit `basics` declaration into existing consumers). Discovery is structural — any `packs/<name>/pack.mjs` is a pack. Each pack's `README.md` lists its rules with a ≤5-word description and whether each is **hardcoded** (a check) or **prose**.
4	
5	## Packs
6	
7	| Pack | Active when | Checks | Prose rules |
8	|---|---|---|---|
9	| [basics](basics/README.md) | declared (seeded by `--init`) | 11 | ~8 (working-discipline + task-lifecycle) |
10	| [barriers](barriers/README.md) | declared (or pulled in via `requires`) | 1 | 0 (config-driven segregation) |
11	| [git-github](git-github/README.md) | pulled in via `basics` `requires` | 0 | 0 (2 skills: git-github-advanced, merge-to-main) |
12	| [grow_with_claudinite](grow_with_claudinite/README.md) | declared (seeded by `--init`, opt-out by removal) | 1 | growth member-side daily tasks (extract / dedup / pack discovery / conversation-extract) + in-session merge capture |
13	| [tidy-repo](tidy-repo/README.md) | declared (seeded by `--init`, opt-out by removal) | 0 | policy (assess-only-vs-act) + tidy daily tasks |
14	| [sheepdog](sheepdog/README.md) | declared (opt-in; the fleet-enforcer repo only) | 0 | fleet-enforcer marker + config + coverage workflow stub |
15	| [github-actions](github-actions/README.md) | `.github/workflows/` | 8 | 0 |
16	| [chrome-extension](chrome-extension/README.md) | manifest_version manifest | 0 | 8 |
